claim: During mammalian development, the left and right ventricles arise from early populations of cardiac progenitors known as the first and second heart fields, respectively.
source: During mammalian development, the left and right ventricles arise from early populations of cardiac progenitors known as the first and second heart fields, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations to prior work in the field of cardiac development.

claim: The first and second heart field populations have been extensively studied in non-human model systems.
source: While these populations have been extensively studied in non-human model systems, their identification and study in vivo human tissues have been limited due to the ethical and technical limitations of accessing gastrulation-stage human embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and implied by the extensive literature on heart field development in animal models.

claim: Identification and study of first and second heart field populations in vivo human tissues have been limited due to ethical and technical limitations of accessing gastrulation-stage human embryos.
source: While these populations have been extensively studied in non-human model systems, their identification and study in vivo human tissues have been limited due to the ethical and technical limitations of accessing gastrulation-stage human embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the limitations of human embryo research.

claim: Human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) have a well-established ability to differentiate into all embryonic germ layers.
source: Human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) present an exciting alternative for modeling early human embryogenesis due to their well-established ability to differentiate into all embryonic germ layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about hiPSC capabilities.

claim: A TBX5/MYL2 lineage tracing reporter system allows for the identification of FHF-progenitors and their descendants including left ventricular cardiomyocytes.
source: Here, we describe the development of a TBX5/MYL2 lineage tracing reporter system that allows for the identification of FHF- progenitors and their descendants including left ventricular cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing the development and validation of the reporter system.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with oligonucleotide-based sample multiplexing was used to extensively profile differentiating hiPSCs across 12 timepoints in two independent iPSC lines.
source: Furthermore, using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with oligonucleotide-based sample multiplexing, we extensively profiled differentiating hiPSCs across 12 timepoints in two independent iPSC lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The reporter system and scRNA-seq analysis revealed a predominance of FHF differentiation using the small molecule Wnt-based 2D differentiation protocol.
source: Surprisingly, our reporter system and scRNA-seq analysis revealed a predominance of FHF differentiation using the small molecule Wnt-based 2D differentiation protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from flow cytometry, qPCR, and scRNA-seq analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: More than 90% of hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes are left ventricular cardiomyocytes.
source: We compared this data with existing murine and 3D cardiac organoid scRNA-seq data and confirmed the dominance of left ventricular cardiomyocytes (>90%) in our hiPSC-derived progeny.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry and scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Critical events in progenitor specification and differentiation occur during the first 3 weeks of human gestation.
source: The human heart is one of the first organs to develop during embryogenesis with critical events in progenitor specification and differentiation occurring during the first 3 weeks of human gestation (Buckingham et al., 2005; Cui et al., 2019; Hikspoors et al., 2022; Meilhac and Buckingham, 2018; Tan and Lewandowski, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Developmental biologists have largely relied upon animal models to study cardiac development due to ethical and technical limitations in the study of human embryogenesis prior to 5 weeks gestation.
source: Due to ethical and technical limitations in the study of human embryogenesis prior to 5 weeks gestation, developmental biologists have largely relied upon animal models to study cardiac development (Hyun et al., 2021; Meilhac and Buckingham, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Early studies in mammalian cardiac progenitor biology identified the presence of two definitive multipotent progenitor populations known as the first (FHF) and second (SHF) heart fields which give rise to the left and right ventricles, respectively.
source: Early studies in mammalian cardiac progenitor biology identified the presence of two definitive multipotent progenitor populations known as the first (FHF) and second (SHF) heart fields which give rise to the left and right ventricles, respectively (Cai et al., 2003; Dyer and Kirby, 2009; Meilhac et al., 2004; Mjaatvedt et al., 2001; Moretti et al., 2006; Waldo et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Early specification of FHF and SHF lineages likely occurs during the earliest stages of gastrulation, with the FHF emerging as the first wave of cardiac progenitors, followed by the SHF.
source: Furthermore, early lineage tracing studies using the mesodermal progenitor marker, Mesp1, has revealed that the early specification of these lineages likely occurs during the earliest stages of gastrulation, with the FHF emerging as the first wave of cardiac progenitors, followed by the SHF (Lescroart et al., 2014; Saga et al., 1999; Scialdone et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior lineage tracing studies.

claim: FHF and SHF progenitor populations have been extensively characterized using scRNA-seq and shown to exhibit unique transcriptional expression profiles.
source: With the advent of scRNA-seq, these progenitor populations have been extensively characterized and shown to exhibit unique transcriptional expression profiles (de Soysa et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior scRNA-seq studies.

claim: Transcriptional differences between murine left and right ventricles can be detected up to E10.5 of murine development.
source: Moreover, scRNA-seq profiling of murine left and right ventricles during early cardiac development has shown that transcriptional differences can be detected up to E10.5 of murine development, suggesting that early left and right ventricular development is characterized by unique transcriptional regulatory networks (DeLaughter et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior scRNA-seq studies of murine cardiac development.

claim: Early left and right ventricular development is characterized by unique transcriptional regulatory networks.
source: Moreover, scRNA-seq profiling of murine left and right ventricles during early cardiac development has shown that transcriptional differences can be detected up to E10.5 of murine development, suggesting that early left and right ventricular development is characterized by unique transcriptional regulatory networks (DeLaughter et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of transcriptional differences and supported by citations.

claim: The identification of first and second heart field progenitor populations within a human model has been severely limited by a lack of access to human embryonic tissues.
source: While the distinct identities of the first and second heart field progenitors have been well established in the murine system, the identification of these progenitor populations within a human model has been severely limited by a lack of access to human embryonic tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about limitations in human embryo research.

claim: The advent of hiPSCs has allowed for the developmental modeling of multiple different embryonic lineages in vitro.
source: Over the past decade, the advent of hiPSCs has allowed for the developmental modeling of multiple different embryonic lineages in vitro (Holloway et al., 2020; Kanton et al., 2019; Karagiannis et al., 2019; Lian et al., 2013; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Yamanaka, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work on hiPSC applications.

claim: Small molecule-based protocols modulating WNT signaling have become standard for cardiac differentiation due to their remarkable efficiency in generating large numbers of beating cardiomyocytes.
source: In the cardiac field, small molecule-based protocols modulating WNT signaling have become standard due to their remarkable efficiency in generating large numbers of beating cardiomyocytes that can be utilized for disease modeling, drug discovery, and the study of cellular functions (Burridge et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Feyen et al., 2020; Lian et al., 2013; Sacchetto et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published protocols and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Questions remain as to whether hiPSC cardiac differentiations are capable of modeling early cardiac progenitor biology as seen during in vivo mouse development.
source: Several questions remain as to whether hiPSC cardiac differentiations are capable of modeling early cardiac progenitor biology as seen during in vivo mouse development (Protze et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work discussing limitations of hiPSC models.

claim: Evidence is lacking as to whether current hiPSC differentiation protocols give rise to FHF- and SHF-derived LV and RV cardiomyocytes, respectively.
source: Moreover, evidence is lacking as to whether current hiPSC differentiation protocols give rise to FHF- and SHF-derived LV and RV cardiomyocytes, respectively (Protze et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work discussing gaps in knowledge.

claim: A major bottleneck in the identification of FHF and SHF cell types during hiPSC differentiation is the lack of lineage tracing tools.
source: A major bottleneck in the identification of these cell types during hiPSC differentiation is the lack of lineage tracing tools that have been extensively used in murine models to understand the developmental lineage contributions of progenitor populations (Barnes et al., 2010; Cai et al., 2003; Meilhac et al., 2004; Moretti et al., 2006; Tyser et al., 2020; Vincentz et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior lineage tracing studies in mice and the inference that such tools are lacking in human systems.

claim: Early studies profiling the expression of TBX5 identified its specific expression at the cardiac crescent and its role as a marker of early FHF progenitors.
source: Early studies profiling the expression of the T-box transcription factor, TBX5, identified its specific expression at the cardiac crescent and its role as a marker of early FHF progenitors (Bruneau et al., 2001; Bruneau et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on TBX5 expression.

claim: Studies using inducible CreER/LoxP lineage tracing have shown the exquisite specificity of TBX5 to label ventricular cardiomyocytes on the left but not the right.
source: More recently, studies using inducible CreER/LoxP lineage tracing have shown the exquisite specificity of TBX5 to label ventricular cardiomyocytes on the left but not the right, demonstrating a clear boundary between cell origins of left and right ventricular cardiomyocytes during embryogenesis (Devine et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior lineage tracing study.

claim: No lineage tracing tool is currently available for tracing LV and RV cardiomyocytes in a human model system.
source: While lineage tracing tools have provided insight into the cellular contributions of the FHF in mice, no lineage tracing tool is currently available for tracing LV and RV cardiomyocytes in a human model system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of such tools in the literature and the motivation for the current study.

claim: A CRISPR-Cas9 targeting platform was used to engineer a TBX5 expression-driven, highly-sensitive, Cre/LoxP lineage tracing system in hiPSCs.
source: To identify FHF-progenitors and their derived cell types during hiPSC differentiation, we used a CRISPR-Cas9 targeting platform to engineer a TBX5 expression-driven, highly-sensitive, Cre/LoxP lineage tracing system in hiPSCs that contain a ventricular cardiomyocyte-specific myosin light chain-2 (MYL2)-tdTomato fluorescent protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The engineered hiPSCs contain a ventricular cardiomyocyte-specific myosin light chain-2 (MYL2)-tdTomato fluorescent protein.
source: To identify FHF-progenitors and their derived cell types during hiPSC differentiation, we used a CRISPR-Cas9 targeting platform to engineer a TBX5 expression-driven, highly-sensitive, Cre/LoxP lineage tracing system in hiPSCs that contain a ventricular cardiomyocyte-specific myosin light chain-2 (MYL2)-tdTomato fluorescent protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Time course analysis of cardiomyocyte differentiation identified a left ventricular cardiomyocyte predominant differentiation across two distinct cell lines based on the high percentage of TBX5-lineage positive ventricular cardiomyocytes (>90%).
source: By conducting a time course analysis of cardiomyocyte differentiation, we identified a left ventricular cardiomyocyte predominant differentiation across two distinct cell lines based on the high percentage of TBX5-lineage positive ventricular cardiomyocytes (>90%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Chemically modified lipid-oligonucleotides (CMOs) were used to conduct multiplexed scRNA-seq assays on 12 different timepoints across two independent hiPSC lines.
source: Using chemically modified lipid-oligonucleotides (CMOs), we conducted multiplexed scRNA-seq assays on 12 different timepoints across two independent hiPSC lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Differentiation trajectory analysis compared scRNA-seq data with murine heart field development scRNA-seq data and validated the FHF origin and LV identity of cardiomyocytes generated.
source: Using differentiation trajectory analysis, we compared our scRNA-seq data with murine heart field development scRNA-seq data and validate the FHF origin and LV identity of cardiomyocytes generated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Comparison of scRNA-seq data with a recently published 3D cardiac organoid differentiation identified the greater potential of a 3D system to generate SHF-derived cell types.
source: Finally, we conduct a comparison of our scRNA-seq data with a recently published 3D cardiac organoid differentiation (Drakhlis et al., 2021) and identify the greater potential of a 3D system to generate SHF-derived cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: The MYL2-tdTomato construct was previously developed and validated to specifically isolate ventricular cardiomyocytes during hiPSC differentiations.
source: Previously, our laboratory developed an MYL2-tdTomato construct targeting a P2A-TdTomato to the stop codon of the MYL2 gene that was validated to specifically isolate ventricular cardiomyocytes during hiPSC differentiations (Chirikian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: A triple construct system was employed to allow for the identification of MYL2-positive ventricular cardiomyocytes and the identification of TBX5-lineage-positive left ventricular cardiomyocytes.
source: To construct a reporter system that could isolate left ventricular cardiomyocytes, we employed a triple construct system that would allow for the identification of MYL2-positive ventricular cardiomyocytes and the identification of TBX5-lineage-positive left ventricular cardiomyocytes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The first construct consists of tandem P2A-Cre Recombinase genes that are targeted to replace the stop codon of TBX5.
source: The first construct consists of tandem P2A-Cre Recombinase genes that are targeted to replace the stop codon of TBX5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The second construct consists of a constitutively active CMV promoter followed by a floxed stop cassette and a downstream TurboGFP.
source: The second construct consists of a constitutively active CMV promoter followed by a floxed stop cassette and a downstream TurboGFP with the goal to only allow for TurboGFP expression after the excision of the stop cassette by Cre (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: TurboGFP expression is only allowed after the excision of the stop cassette by Cre.
source: The second construct consists of a constitutively active CMV promoter followed by a floxed stop cassette and a downstream TurboGFP with the goal to only allow for TurboGFP expression after the excision of the stop cassette by Cre (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on the known mechanism of Cre/LoxP recombination and the experimental design.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing was used to target the MYL2-tdTomato construct into two hiPSC lines derived from healthy donor patients.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we first targeted the MYL2-tdTomato construct into two hiPSC lines derived from healthy donor patients (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods described in the text.

claim: An inside-out PCR strategy was used to confirm the successful integration of the MYL2 construct.
source: Using an inside-out PCR strategy (Galdos et al., 2021; Ran et al., 2013), we confirmed the successful integration of the MYL2 construct based on the integration of the 5' and 3' ends of the construct and selected a heterozygous integrated clone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A heterozygous integrated clone was selected for the MYL2 construct.
source: Using an inside-out PCR strategy (Galdos et al., 2021; Ran et al., 2013), we confirmed the successful integration of the MYL2 construct based on the integration of the 5' and 3' ends of the construct and selected a heterozygous integrated clone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods described in the text.

claim: The CMV-Lox-STOP-Lox-TurboGFP construct was integrated into the CCR5 safe harbor site.
source: We subsequently integrated the CMV-Lox-STOP-Lox-TurboGFP construct into the CCR5 safe harbor site and confirmed successful integration via inside-out PCR (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Successful integration of the CMV-Lox-STOP-Lox-TurboGFP construct was confirmed via inside-out PCR.
source: We subsequently integrated the CMV-Lox-STOP-Lox-TurboGFP construct into the CCR5 safe harbor site and confirmed successful integration via inside-out PCR (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The P2A-Cre-P2A-Cre construct was integrated into the TBX5 locus by replacing the stop codon of the gene.
source: Next, we integrated the P2A-Cre-P2A-Cre construct into the TBX5 locus by replacing the stop codon of the gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods described in the text.

claim: The P2A-Cre construct was integrated in a homozygous manner to ensure high expression of Cre recombinase upon expression of TBX5.
source: To ensure maximal sensitivity of our lineage tracing system, we integrated the P2A-Cre construct in a homozygous manner to ensure high expression of Cre recombinase upon expression of TBX5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design rationale and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expression of TBX5 is preserved with the P2A-Cre integration approach since the Cre recombinase is inserted after the TBX5 coding sequence and the fusion protein product undergoes self-cleaving at the P2A sequence.
source: Importantly, the expression of TBX5 is preserved with this approach since the Cre recombinase is inserted after the TBX5 coding sequence and the fusion protein product undergoes self-cleaving at the P2A sequence (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on the known mechanism of P2A self-cleaving peptides and supported by a citation.

claim: Sanger sequencing validated the in-frame integration of the P2A sequences of both the MYL2 and TBX5 constructs.
source: Using sanger sequencing, we validated the in-frame integration of the P2A sequences of both the MYL2 and TBX5 constructs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The maintenance of pluripotency after three rounds of genome editing was confirmed by immunostaining of pluripotency markers OCT4, NANOG, and TRA-1-8-1.
source: Lastly, we confirmed the maintenance of pluripotency after three rounds of genome editing by immunostaining of pluripotency marker OCT4, NANOG, and TRA-1-8-1 (Figure 1E), thus demonstrating the successful genome editing of three independent genetic constructs into two different hiPSC lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Three independent genetic constructs were successfully genome edited into two different hiPSC lines.
source: Lastly, we confirmed the maintenance of pluripotency after three rounds of genome editing by immunostaining of pluripotency marker OCT4, NANOG, and TRA-1-8-1 (Figure 1E), thus demonstrating the successful genome editing of three independent genetic constructs into two different hiPSC lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cumulative experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cardiac differentiations were conducted using a widely published differentiation protocol consisting of biphasic activation and subsequent inhibition of WNT signaling using small molecules.
source: To determine the proportion of hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes that exhibit a TBX5-lineage positive phenotype, we conducted cardiac differentiations using a widely published differentiation protocol consisting of biphasic activation and subsequent inhibition of WNT signaling using small molecules (Figure 1A, see Methods; Lian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described and a citation to the original protocol.

claim: High throughput flow cytometry analysis of cardiac troponin, TurboGFP, and tdTomato expression was conducted across multiple timepoints during cardiac differentiation and across the two independent cell lines.
source: We employed a strategy where we conducted a high throughput flow cytometry analysis of cardiac troponin, TurboGFP, and tdTomato expression across multiple timepoints during cardiac differentiation and across the two independent cell lines containing our reporter system (Figure 2A, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Analysis of TNNT2 expression from day 3 to 30 of differentiation revealed a gradual upregulation of TNNT2 expression starting at day 7 of differentiation.
source: Analysis of TNNT2 expression from day 3 to 30 of differentiation revealed a gradual upregulation of TNNT2 expression starting at day 7 of differentiation (Figure 2B and D), with the greatest increase in TNNT2+ cardiomyocytes being reported between day 7 and 11 of differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: The greatest increase in TNNT2+ cardiomyocytes was reported between day 7 and 11 of differentiation.
source: Analysis of TNNT2 expression from day 3 to 30 of differentiation revealed a gradual upregulation of TNNT2 expression starting at day 7 of differentiation (Figure 2B and D), with the greatest increase in TNNT2+ cardiomyocytes being reported between day 7 and 11 of differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Overall cardiac differentiation at day 30 across both reporter lines (WTC and SCVI-111) averaged 93.2 ± 0.80% and 92.1 ± 1.60% of TNNT2+ cells out of the total cells analyzed, respectively.
source: Overall cardiac differentiation at day 30 across both reporter lines (WTC and SCVI-111) averaged 93.2 ± 0.80% and 92.1 ± 1.60% of TNNT2+ cells out of the total cells analyzed, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A large increase in TurboGFP+ cells was found between days 7 and 11 with a continuous increase in the level of GFP signal as the differentiation proceeded.
source: We further analyzed the proportion of cells that were positive for TurboGFP + between day 3 and 30 of differentiation (Figure 2B and E) and found a large increase in TurboGFP + cells between days 7 and 11 with a continuous increase in the level of GFP signal as the differentiation proceeded.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and E.

claim: By day 30, both WTC and SCVI-111 lines exhibited 99.0 ± 0.21% and 93.2 ± 0.84% of total TNNT2+ cardiomyocytes expressing TurboGFP, respectively.
source: By day 30, both WTC and SCVI-111 lines exhibited 99.0 ± 0.21% and 93.2 ± 0.84% of total TNNT2 + cardiomyocytes expressing TurboGFP, respectively, indicating a predominance of cardiomyocytes from the TBX5 lineage (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The high percentage of TurboGFP+ cardiomyocytes indicates a predominance of cardiomyocytes from the TBX5 lineage.
source: By day 30, both WTC and SCVI-111 lines exhibited 99.0 ± 0.21% and 93.2 ± 0.84% of total TNNT2 + cardiomyocytes expressing TurboGFP, respectively, indicating a predominance of cardiomyocytes from the TBX5 lineage (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the flow cytometry data and the design of the lineage tracing system.

claim: TBX5 is known to be expressed in both atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes.
source: Since TBX5 is known to be expressed in both atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes, we next determined the percentage of ventricular cardiomyocytes that are within the TBX5-lineage by analyzing the proportion of MYL2-tdTomato+ cardiomyocytes that express TurboGFP.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: MYL2 expression gradually increases over time during both hiPSC cardiac differentiation and in vivo development and is highly tied to the overall maturational status of hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes.
source: MYL2 expression gradually increases over time during both hiPSC cardiac differentiation and in vivo development and is highly tied to the overall maturational status of hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (Bizy et al., 2013; Chirikian et al., 2021; DeLaughter et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016; O'Brien et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The percentage of MYL2-tdTomato+ cardiomyocytes increases between days 15 and 30 of cardiomyocyte differentiation.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we show that the percentage of MYL2-tdTomato+ cardiomyocytes increases between days 15 and 30 of cardiomyocyte differentiation with some line-to-line variability likely tied to variation in hiPSC-CM maturation rate thus accounting for the higher percentage seen in the WTC line over the SCVI-111 (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: Line-to-line variability in MYL2-tdTomato+ cardiomyocytes is likely tied to variation in hiPSC-CM maturation rate.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we show that the percentage of MYL2-tdTomato+ cardiomyocytes increases between days 15 and 30 of cardiomyocyte differentiation with some line-to-line variability likely tied to variation in hiPSC-CM maturation rate thus accounting for the higher percentage seen in the WTC line over the SCVI-111 (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed variability and knowledge about hiPSC-CM maturation.

claim: Across day 15, 20, and 30, for both cell lines, the proportion of ventricular cardiomyocytes marked by the tdTomato reporter were more than 95% for TurboGFP.
source: Across day 15, 20, and 30 we observed that for both cell lines, the proportion of ventricular cardiomyocytes marked by the tdTomato reporter were more than 95% for TurboGFP indicating that nearly all ventricular cardiomyocytes were within the TBX5-lineage (Figure 2F, Figure 2G, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2F, 2G, and 3A.

claim: Nearly all ventricular cardiomyocytes were within the TBX5-lineage.
source: Across day 15, 20, and 30 we observed that for both cell lines, the proportion of ventricular cardiomyocytes marked by the tdTomato reporter were more than 95% for TurboGFP indicating that nearly all ventricular cardiomyocytes were within the TBX5-lineage (Figure 2F, Figure 2G, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the high percentage of TurboGFP+ ventricular cardiomyocytes.

claim: Bulk gene expression analyses using RT-qPCR were conducted across multiple timepoints during hiPSC differentiation to validate the expression kinetics of the reporter system.
source: We further validated the expression kinetics of our reporter system by conducting bulk gene expression analyses using RT-qPCR across multiple timepoints during hiPSC differentiation (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: HAND1 and TBX5 are known markers of early FHF progenitors and left ventricular cardiomyocytes.
source: We evaluated the expression of known markers of early FHF progenitors and left ventricular cardiomyocytes, HAND1 and TBX5 (Barnes et al., 2010; de Soysa et al., 2019; Devine et al., 2014; Vincentz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: HAND1 exhibited more than 50,000 fold upregulation relative to day 0 by day 7 of differentiation across both lines.
source: Relative to day 0 we observed that all three markers exhibited high expression values with HAND1 exhibiting more than 50,000 fold upregulation relative to day 0 by day 7 of differentiation across both lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: By day 30 of differentiation, TBX5 exhibited nearly 3000-fold upregulation relative to day 0.
source: Similarly, by day 30 of differentiation, TBX5 exhibited nearly 3000-fold upregulation relative to day 0 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The expression of Cre recombinase increased over time and was consistent with the expected increase in TurboGFP expression observed in the flow cytometry data.
source: The expression of Cre recombinase increased over time and was consistent with the expected increase in TurboGFP expression observed in the flow cytometry data (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and comparison with flow cytometry data.

claim: ISL1, FGF8, and TBX1 are SHF markers.
source: In addition to analyzing FHF marker expression, we also examined the expression of SHF markers such as ISL1, FGF8, and TBX1 (Figure 3C; Cai et al., 2003; Park et al., 2008; Rana et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: ISL1 has been reported to be expressed in the early FHF lineage.
source: While ISL1 has been reported to be expressed in the early FHF lineage (Ma et al., 2008), a well-established observation is that ISL1 expression is sustained during the emergence of the SHF (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: ISL1 expression is sustained during the emergence of the SHF.
source: While ISL1 has been reported to be expressed in the early FHF lineage (Ma et al., 2008), a well-established observation is that ISL1 expression is sustained during the emergence of the SHF (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: In both the WTC and SCVI-111 lines, ISL1 expression peaked at day 5 of differentiation, which is indicative of an early cardiac progenitor population at that timepoint.
source: Interestingly, we observed in both the WTC and SCVI-111 that ISL1 expression peaked at day 5 of differentiation, which is indicative of an early cardiac progenitor population at that timepoint.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data and inference about the cell population.

claim: A sustained expression of ISL1 was not observed and rather its downregulation over time was observed.
source: We did not observe a sustained expression of ISL1 and rather observed its downregulation over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: FGF8 has been reported to be important for early cardiomyocyte differentiation in both the FHF and SHF.
source: Similarly, FGF8 has been reported to be important for early cardiomyocyte differentiation in both the FHF and SHF, however, its expression is maintained within SHF progenitors during cardiogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: FGF8 expression is maintained within SHF progenitors during cardiogenesis.
source: Similarly, FGF8 has been reported to be important for early cardiomyocyte differentiation in both the FHF and SHF, however, its expression is maintained within SHF progenitors during cardiogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: While FGF8 expression was present at the mesodermal stage of differentiation, a significant drop in expression was observed after day 7.
source: We observed that while FGF8 expression was present at the mesodermal stage of differentiation (Figure 3C), a significant drop in expression was observed after day 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TBX1 is a pharyngeal endoderm and mesoderm marker.
source: TBX1, a pharyngeal endoderm and mesoderm marker (Chapman et al., 1996; Mesbah et al., 2012; Rana et al., 2014; Vitelli et al., 2002), also known as a marker of the anterior second heart field (Liao et al., 2008; Meilhac and Buckingham, 2018; Nevis et al., 2013), was unexpectedly upregulated during gastrulation and early cardiac progenitor stages of differentiation but declined after day 7 of differentiation with some line-to-line and batch-to-batch variability (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: TBX1 is also known as a marker of the anterior second heart field.
source: TBX1, a pharyngeal endoderm and mesoderm marker (Chapman et al., 1996; Mesbah et al., 2012; Rana et al., 2014; Vitelli et al., 2002), also known as a marker of the anterior second heart field (Liao et al., 2008; Meilhac and Buckingham, 2018; Nevis et al., 2013), was unexpectedly upregulated during gastrulation and early cardiac progenitor stages of differentiation but declined after day 7 of differentiation with some line-to-line and batch-to-batch variability (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: TBX1 was unexpectedly upregulated during gastrulation and early cardiac progenitor stages of differentiation but declined after day 7 of differentiation with some line-to-line and batch-to-batch variability.
source: TBX1, a pharyngeal endoderm and mesoderm marker (Chapman et al., 1996; Mesbah et al., 2012; Rana et al., 2014; Vitelli et al., 2002), also known as a marker of the anterior second heart field (Liao et al., 2008; Meilhac and Buckingham, 2018; Nevis et al., 2013), was unexpectedly upregulated during gastrulation and early cardiac progenitor stages of differentiation but declined after day 7 of differentiation with some line-to-line and batch-to-batch variability (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TBX1 was not upregulated to the same degree as either HAND1 or TBX5, both of which exhibited greater than 1000-fold upregulation in both lines analyzed.
source: Importantly, TBX1 was not upregulated to the same degree as either HAND1 or TBX5, both of which exhibited greater than 1000-fold upregulation in both lines analyzed.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RT-qPCR data for different genes.

claim: The lack of SHF markers upregulation after day 7 contrasts with the continued or even increased expression of FHF markers HAND1 and TBX5, thus indicating the predominance of FHF-derived cells at later stages of differentiation.
source: This lack of SHF markers upregulation after day 7 contrasts with the continued or even increased expression of FHF markers HAND1 and TBX5, thus indicating the predominance of FHF-derived cells at later stages of differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of gene expression patterns.

claim: The fold change expression of TBX1 and ISL1 was significantly lower than that of HAND1 and TBX5, with the FHF markers exhibiting more than 100,000- and 1000-fold increases, respectively.
source: Notably, the fold change expression of TBX1 and ISL1 was significantly lower than that of HAND1 and TBX5, with the FHF markers exhibiting more than 100,000- and 1000-fold increases, respectively (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 2B and C (likely referring to Figure 3B and C).

claim: An increase in cardiomyocyte maturation markers such as TNNT2, MYL2, and MYH7 was observed indicating the reporter lines fully differentiated into beating cardiomyocytes.
source: Lastly, we also observed an increase in cardiomyocyte maturation markers such as TNNT2, MYL2, and MYH7 (Figure 3E) indicating the reporter lines fully differentiated into beating cardiomyocytes (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and videos of beating cardiomyocytes.

claim: A gradual upregulation of MYL2 through the course of hiPSC cardiac differentiation was observed, consistent with flow cytometry data.
source: Consistent with our flow cytometry data, we also observe a gradual upregulation of MYL2 through the course of hiPSC cardiac differentiation. (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data and comparison with flow cytometry data.

claim: The Cre/LoxP-based fluorescent reporter system showed a predominance of TBX5-lineage cardiomyocytes.
source: Given that our Cre/LoxP-based fluorescent reporter system showed a predominance of TBX5-lineage cardiomyocytes (Figure 2E) and our qPCR data showed an upregulation of FHF, but not SHF, gene markers at late stages of differentiation (Figure 3B and C), we asked whether scRNA-seq may help to pinpoint the developmental trajectories that bifurcate between FHF and SHF during hiPSC differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: qPCR data showed an upregulation of FHF, but not SHF, gene markers at late stages of differentiation.
source: Given that our Cre/LoxP-based fluorescent reporter system showed a predominance of TBX5-lineage cardiomyocytes (Figure 2E) and our qPCR data showed an upregulation of FHF, but not SHF, gene markers at late stages of differentiation (Figure 3B and C), we asked whether scRNA-seq may help to pinpoint the developmental trajectories that bifurcate between FHF and SHF during hiPSC differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 3B and C.

claim: Sample multiplexing with CMO was used in the scRNA-seq experiment where cells were captured from both the WTC and SCVI-111 lines and at 12 different timepoints of hiPSC cardiac differentiation (Days 0–7 and 11, 13, 15, and 30) for a total of 27,595 cells after sample demultiplexing and quality control.
source: Using sample multiplexing with CMO in our scRNA-seq experiment where we captured cells from both the WTC and SCVI-111 lines and at 12 different timepoints hiPSC cardiac differentiation (Days 0–7 and 11, 13, 15, and 30) for a total of 27,595 cells after sample demultiplexing and quality control (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: The mutual nearest neighbor algorithm was used to batch-correct the effect of the scRNA-seq runs.
source: Using a well-published batch correction method known as the mutual nearest neighbor algorithm (Haghverdi et al., 2018), we batch-corrected the effect of the scRNA-seq runs and conducted downstream dimensionality reduction and unsupervised clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described and a citation to the algorithm.

claim: Annotation of unsupervised clusters revealed 13 major populations during cardiac differentiation.
source: Annotation of unsupervised clusters revealed 13 major populations during cardiac differentiation (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: During the early days of differentiation, cell populations consistent with pluripotent stem cells, primitive streak, and definitive endoderm populations were identified marked by the expression of POU5F1, MIXL1, and SOX17, respectively.
source: During the early days of differentiation we identified cell populations consistent with pluripotent stem cells, primitive streak, and definitive endoderm populations marked by the expression of POU5F1, MIXL1, and SOX17, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—source data 2; Mead et al., 1996; Pijuan-Sala et al., 2019; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Tyser et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the scRNA-seq data and citations to prior work on these markers.

claim: By day 3 of differentiation, the emergence of mesodermal progenitors, early cardiac progenitors, late cardiac progenitors, cardiomyocytes, and epicardial populations was observed marked by the expression of MESP1, ISL1, NKX2-5, TNNT2, and WT1, respectively.
source: By day 3 of differentiation, we observed the emergence of mesodermal progenitors, early cardiac progenitors, late cardiac progenitors, cardiomyocytes, and epicardial populations marked by the expression of MESP1, ISL1, NKX2-5, TNNT2, and WT1, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—source data 2; Barnes et al., 2010; Christoffels et al., 2009; Rudat and Kispert, 2012; Zeng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the scRNA-seq data and citations to prior work on these markers.

claim: The STREAM algorithm was used to automatically identify and visualize differentiation trajectories within the scRNA-seq data.
source: We used a Python-based bioinformatic pipeline known as STREAM to automatically identify and visualize differentiation trajectories within our scRNA-seq data (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described and a citation to the STREAM algorithm.

claim: STREAM uses a low-dimensional manifold such as a UMAP plot and calculates a principal graph that identifies differentiation paths throughout the dataset.
source: STREAM uses a low-dimensional manifold such as a UMAP plot and calculates a principal graph that identifies differentiation paths throughout the dataset.
evidence: This claim is based on the known functionality of the STREAM algorithm.

claim: The STREAM algorithm fits a principal graph that identified two major bifurcations during hiPSC differentiation.
source: Intriguingly, the STREAM algorithm fits a principal graph that identified two major bifurcations during hiPSC differentiation (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis shown in Figure 4D and supplementary figures.

claim: STREAM pseudotime was calculated by setting the pluripotent stem cell cluster as the root of the differentiation.
source: Along with the fitting of a principal graph, we calculated STREAM pseudotime by setting the pluripotent stem cell cluster as the root of the differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described for STREAM analysis.

claim: Cells were reordered and projected along the principal graph according to increasing pseudotime to visualize annotated cell types as they progressed during differentiation.
source: We then reordered and projected cells along the principal graph according to increasing pseudotime to visualize our annotated cell types as they progressed during differentiation (Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis shown in Figure 4D-F and supplementary figures.

claim: The expression of gene expression was correlated with the cell pseudotime along each unique branch to further characterize the distinct trajectories identified by STREAM.
source: To further characterize the distinct trajectories identified by STREAM, we correlated the expression of gene expression with the cell pseudotime along each unique branch (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described for STREAM analysis.

claim: The analysis recovered multiple gene markers known to be expressed during the course of gastrulation and cardiac development.
source: This analysis recovered multiple gene markers known to be expressed during the course of gastrulation and cardiac development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis results and comparison with known markers.

claim: The first bifurcation identified occurred at the late primitive streak stage and represents the bifurcation into mesodermal and endodermal cell lineages.
source: The first bifurcation identified occurred at the late primitive streak stage and represents the bifurcation into mesodermal and endodermal cell lineages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the STREAM analysis and known developmental biology.

claim: Gene markers identified for the endodermal lineage include markers such as EPCAM and FOXA2, as well as hepatic-like endodermal markers such as APOA1 and AFP.
source: Gene markers identified for the endodermal lineage include markers such as EPCAM and FOXA2, as well as hepatic-like endodermal markers such as APOA1 and AFP (Figure 4G; Hurrell et al., 2019; Pijuan-Sala et al., 2019; Sarrach et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis shown in Figure 4G and citations to prior work on these markers.

claim: Along the mesodermal differentiation path, the upregulation of MESP1 followed by ISL1 expression was observed as cells became specified along the cardiac progenitor lineage.
source: Along the mesodermal differentiation path, we observed the upregulation of MESP1 followed by ISL1 expression as cells became specified along the cardiac progenitor lineage.
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis results.

claim: ISL1 expression preceded the expression of NKX2-5 and encompasses both endodermal precursors as well as cardiac progenitors, supporting the earlier but less cardiac-specific expression of ISL1.
source: ISL1 expression preceded the expression of NKX2-5 and encompasses both endodermal precursors as well as cardiac progenitors, supporting the earlier but less cardiac-specific expression of ISL1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis results and inference about ISL1 expression patterns.

claim: At the second bifurcation, an NKX2-5 population was identified that bifurcated into myocardial and epicardial lineages.
source: At the second bifurcation, we identified an NKX2-5 population that bifurcated into myocardial and epicardial lineages.
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis results.

claim: Top ranking markers for the epicardial lineage included known epicardial markers TBX18, WT1, TCF21, and IGF2.
source: Top ranking markers for the epicardial lineage included known epicardial markers TBX18, WT1, TCF21, and IGF2, while the myocardial lineage was characterized by the elevated expression of sarcomeric genes (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5D; Christoffels et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2011; Rudat and Kispert, 2012; Tandon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis shown in Figure 4G and supplementary figures, and citations to prior work on these markers.

claim: The myocardial lineage was characterized by the elevated expression of sarcomeric genes.
source: Top ranking markers for the epicardial lineage included known epicardial markers TBX18, WT1, TCF21, and IGF2, while the myocardial lineage was characterized by the elevated expression of sarcomeric genes (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5D; Christoffels et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2011; Rudat and Kispert, 2012; Tandon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis shown in Figure 4G and supplementary figures.

claim: Within the epicardial lineage, a high expression of HAND1 along with the enrichment of extracellular matrix genes such as COL3A1, VIM, and COL1A1 was observed at the epicardial progenitor population, suggesting the emergence of WT1 positive epicardial cells from a HAND1 expressing precursor.
source: Within the epicardial lineage, we observed a high expression of HAND1 along with the enrichment of extracellular matrix genes such as COL3A1, VIM, and COL1A1 at the epicardial progenitor population, suggesting the emergence of WT1 positive epicardial cells from a HAND1 expressing precursor (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis results and inference about cell lineage relationships.

claim: STREAM revealed the emergence of an epicardial and myocardial lineage from a common cardiac progenitor during hiPSC differentiation.
source: Together, STREAM revealed the emergence of an epicardial and myocardial lineage from a common cardiac progenitor during hiPSC differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the STREAM analysis results.

claim: A comparison was conducted between previously published murine scRNA-seq heart field data and hiPSC cardiac differentiation data to confirm the FHF cardiomyocyte-predominant differentiation of hiPSCs.
source: To confirm the FHF cardiomyocyte-predominant differentiation of hiPSCs that we observed in our TBX5 lineage tracing (Figure 2D) and qPCR (Figure 3B and C) data, we conducted a comparison between previously published murine scRNA-seq heart field data (de Soysa et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2019; Pijuan-Sala et al., 2019) and our hiPSC cardiac differentiation data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis methods described and citations to prior murine datasets.

claim: Data from the murine datasets representing seven major cell types of interest including nascent mesoderm, heart field progenitors, epicardial cells, left and right ventricular cardiomyocytes, and outflow tract cardiomyocytes were clustered.
source: We clustered data from the murine datasets representing seven major cell types of interest including nascent mesoderm, heart field progenitors, epicardial cells, left and right ventricular cardiomyocytes, and outflow tract cardiomyocytes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A bifurcation of the FHF and SHF cells from the nascent mesoderm was observed in the murine data.
source: As previously reported (de Soysa et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2019), we observed a bifurcation of the FHF and SHF cells from the nascent mesoderm and observed a clear contribution of both heart field progenitors to the development of left and right ventricular cardiomyocytes with FHF cells contributing to the LV and SHF cells contributing to the RV/OFT.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: A clear contribution of both heart field progenitors to the development of left and right ventricular cardiomyocytes was observed with FHF cells contributing to the LV and SHF cells contributing to the RV/OFT in the murine data.
source: As previously reported (de Soysa et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2019), we observed a bifurcation of the FHF and SHF cells from the nascent mesoderm and observed a clear contribution of both heart field progenitors to the development of left and right ventricular cardiomyocytes with FHF cells contributing to the LV and SHF cells contributing to the RV/OFT.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: The epicardial lineage branched off from FHF progenitor cells in the murine data.
source: Intriguingly, we observed the epicardial lineage branched off from FHF progenitor cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: This observation is consistent with the recent lineage tracing literature that indicates the contribution of a subset of FHF progenitors to both left ventricular cardiomyocytes as well as epicardial cells.
source: This observation is consistent with the recent lineage tracing literature that indicates the contribution of a subset of FHF progenitors to both left ventricular cardiomyocytes as well as epicardial cells (Tyser et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent lineage tracing studies.

claim: TBX5 and HCN4 were upregulated in FHF cells during mouse development in vivo and are completely absent in the aSHF lineage.
source: Consistent with the literature, TBX5 and HCN4 were upregulated in FHF cells during mouse development in vivo and are completely absent in the aSHF lineage (Figure 5C; Andersen et al., 2018; Bruneau et al., 2001; Devine et al., 2014; Später et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5C and citations to prior work.

claim: Tbx5 appeared to gradually increase in expression during the transition from FHF progenitors to LV CMs with a gradual downregulation as development progresses, indicating a dynamic expression pattern through the course of development.
source: Of note, Tbx5 appeared to gradually increase in expression during the transition from FHF progenitors to LV CMs with a gradual downregulation as development progresses, indicating a dynamic expression pattern through the course of development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis of murine data.

claim: A clear upregulation of aSHF markers TBX1 and FGF8 was observed during early aSHF progenitor development in mice.
source: In contrast to the FHF markers, we observed a clear upregulation of aSHF markers TBX1 and FGF8 during early aSHF progenitor development in mice with Fgf8 exhibiting its highest expression pattern at prior to the bifurcation between OFT CM and RV CM (Figure 5C; Nevis et al., 2013; Park et al., 2008; Vitelli et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5C and citations to prior work.

claim: Fgf8 exhibited its highest expression pattern prior to the bifurcation between OFT CM and RV CM in mice.
source: In contrast to the FHF markers, we observed a clear upregulation of aSHF markers TBX1 and FGF8 during early aSHF progenitor development in mice with Fgf8 exhibiting its highest expression pattern at prior to the bifurcation between OFT CM and RV CM (Figure 5C; Nevis et al., 2013; Park et al., 2008; Vitelli et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The expression of TBX1 and FGF8 was absent in FHF progenitors, albeit a low Fgf8 expression was found in early LV CM, which is expected given the role of Fgf signaling during early cardiomyocyte differentiation.
source: As expected, the expression of TBX1 and FGF8 was absent in FHF progenitors, albeit a low Fgf8 expression was found in early LV CM, which is expected given the role of Fgf signaling during early cardiomyocyte differentiation (Khosravi et al., 2021; Reifers et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis and citations to prior work on Fgf signaling.

claim: A striking consistency in marker expression with the FHF lineage in the mouse was observed when plotting the expression of FHF and SHF markers during hiPSC cardiac differentiations.
source: We next plotted the expression of these markers during our hiPSC cardiac differentiations and observed a striking consistency in marker expression with the FHF lineage in the mouse (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The upregulation of TBX5 starting at the late progenitor stage and increasing during the myocardial branch of the differentiation was observed, like the kinetics observed in the FHF trajectory of the mouse.
source: Importantly, we observed the upregulation of TBX5 starting at the late progenitor stage and increasing during the myocardial branch of the differentiation, like the kinetics observed in the FHF trajectory of the mouse (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HCN4 expression remained high during cardiomyocyte differentiation further supporting the left ventricular identity of the myocardial branch given the reported role of HCN4 as an early FHF and LV marker.
source: Similarly, HCN4 expression remained high during cardiomyocyte differentiation further supporting the left ventricular identity of the myocardial branch given the reported role of HCN4 as an early FHF and LV marker (Später et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis and a citation to prior work on HCN4.

claim: The ventricular-specific trajectory of hiPSC differentiation was confirmed given the gradual upregulation of the ventricular-specific Iroquois transcription factor, IRX4.
source: We confirmed the ventricular-specific trajectory of our hiPSC differentiation given the gradual upregulation of the ventricular-specific Iroquois transcription factor, IRX4 (Figure 5E; Nelson et al., 2016; Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 5E and citations to prior work on IRX4.

claim: Previous studies have shown IRX4 to mark early ventricular-specific cardiomyocytes.
source: Previous studies have shown IRX4 to mark early ventricular-specific cardiomyocytes, which we effectively observed in both the left and right ventricular differentiation lineages in the murine data (Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on IRX4.

claim: IRX4 was effectively observed in both the left and right ventricular differentiation lineages in the murine data.
source: Previous studies have shown IRX4 to mark early ventricular-specific cardiomyocytes, which we effectively observed in both the left and right ventricular differentiation lineages in the murine data (Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis of murine data.

claim: The ventricular-specific differentiation of hiPSC-derived CMs was further confirmed by observing the absence of atrial markers, KCNA5, NR2F1, and VSNL1.
source: We further confirmed the ventricular-specific differentiation of our hiPSC-derived CMs by observing the absence of atrial markers, KCNA5, NR2F1, and VSNL1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7D.

claim: Consistent with the MYL2-tdtomato expression pattern observed with the reporter lines, the gradual upregulation of MYL2 was observed in both the human and murine datasets.
source: Lastly, consistent with the MYL2-tdtomato expression pattern observed with our reporter lines (Figure 2F), we observed the gradual upregulation of MYL2 in both the human and murine datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis and comparison with reporter data.

claim: The analysis provides evidence for the predominance of FHF ventricular cardiomyocyte development during hiPSC differentiation.
source: Together, our analysis provides evidence for the predominance of FHF ventricular cardiomyocyte development during hiPSC differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cumulative comparative analysis results.

claim: Multiple groups have proposed the use of 3D differentiation to better model chamber morphogenesis and potentially model both first and second heart field development in vitro.
source: Recently, multiple groups have proposed the use of 3D differentiation to better model chamber morphogenesis and potentially model both first and second heart field development in vitro (Andersen et al., 2018; Drakhlis et al., 2021; Protze et al., 2019; Rossi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent publications on 3D cardiac differentiation.

claim: Murine gastruloid and precardiac organoids have been shown to exhibit aspects of first and second heart field development.
source: Interestingly, murine gastruloid and precardiac organoids have been shown to exhibit aspects of first and second heart field development (Andersen et al., 2018; Rossi et al., 2021); however, data on the ability to generate both heart fields in human iPSCs are lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on murine organoids.

claim: Data on the ability to generate both heart fields in human iPSCs are lacking.
source: Interestingly, murine gastruloid and precardiac organoids have been shown to exhibit aspects of first and second heart field development (Andersen et al., 2018; Rossi et al., 2021); however, data on the ability to generate both heart fields in human iPSCs are lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of such data in the literature.

claim: scRNA-seq data from a recently published cardiac organoid study was analyzed to assess whether a greater repertoire of cardiac cells can be generated from a 3D hiPSC differentiation platform.
source: Given the predominance of FHF progenitors and LV cardiomyocytes made from our 2D hiPSC differentiation platform, we assessed whether a greater repertoire of cardiac cells can be generated from a 3D hiPSC differentiation platform by analyzing scRNA-seq data from a recently published cardiac organoid study (Drakhlis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis methods described and a citation to the organoid study.

claim: The Drakhlis et al. paper demonstrated the close relationship between anterior endoderm lineages and anterior second heart field cells during hiPSC differentiation by showing that anterior foregut endoderm can be generated alongside cardiac lineage cell types.
source: This paper demonstrated the close relationship between anterior endoderm lineages and anterior second heart field cells during hiPSC differentiation by showing that anterior foregut endoderm can be generated alongside cardiac lineage cell types (Kelly et al., 2001; Rochais et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the Drakhlis et al. study and citations to related work.

claim: A cross-dataset comparison of FHF and SHF marker analysis was conducted focusing exclusively on cell types composing the myocardial lineages of both datasets.
source: We first conducted a cross-dataset comparison of FHF and SHF marker analysis where we focused exclusively on cell types composing the myocardial lineages of both datasets (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis methods shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the 2D cardiac differentiation, a clear increased expression of FHF markers TBX5, HCN4, and HAND1 during differentiation was observed with the absence of SHF markers FGF8 and TBX1.
source: In our 2D cardiac differentiation, we observed a clear increased expression of FHF markers TBX5, HCN4, and HAND1 during differentiation with the absence of SHF markers FGF8 and TBX1 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The day 13 data from Drakhlis et al. showed two clusters exhibiting distinct transcriptional expression patterns suggestive of FHF and SHF progenitors.
source: Interestingly, the day 13 data from Drakhlis et al., showed two clusters exhibiting distinct transcriptional expression patterns suggestive of FHF and SHF progenitors (Figure 6D), with both clusters appearing to give rise to TNNI1 and NKX2-5 positive cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both clusters in the Drakhlis et al. data appeared to give rise to TNNI1 and NKX2-5 positive cardiomyocytes.
source: Interestingly, the day 13 data from Drakhlis et al., showed two clusters exhibiting distinct transcriptional expression patterns suggestive of FHF and SHF progenitors (Figure 6D), with both clusters appearing to give rise to TNNI1 and NKX2-5 positive cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cluster 2 and 8 of the cardiac organoid data indicated a high expression of TBX5, HAND1, along with the upregulation of HCN4 during differentiation which was consistent with the FHF trajectory observed in the 2D data.
source: Cluster 2 and 8 of the cardiac organoid data indicated a high expression of TBX5, HAND1, along with the upregulation of HCN4 during differentiation which was consistent with the FHF trajectory we observed in our 2D data (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cells in clusters 4, 7, and 10 of Drakhlis et al. exhibited a high expression of TBX1, FGF8, and ISL1, all of which were consistent with a SHF identity.
source: Interestingly, we found that cells in clusters 4, 7, and 10 of Drakhlis et al., exhibited a high expression of TBX1, FGF8, and ISL1, all of which were consistent with a SHF identity (Cai et al., 2003; Mesbah et al., 2012; Park et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis and citations to prior work on SHF markers.

claim: A cardiomyocyte population emerging from the TBX1+ population was observed that was negative for FHF markers TBX5 and HCN4, but highly expressing ISL1 and HAND1, which is suggestive of an OFT CM population.
source: Moreover, we also observed a cardiomyocyte population emerging from the TBX1+ population that was negative for FHF markers TBX5 and HCN4, but highly expressing ISL1 and HAND1, which is suggestive of an OFT CM population that is known to express HAND1 and emerge from ISL1 expressing SHF progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis and inference about cell identity based on marker expression.

claim: OFT CM populations are known to express HAND1 and emerge from ISL1 expressing SHF progenitors.
source: Moreover, we also observed a cardiomyocyte population emerging from the TBX1+ population that was negative for FHF markers TBX5 and HCN4, but highly expressing ISL1 and HAND1, which is suggestive of an OFT CM population that is known to express HAND1 and emerge from ISL1 expressing SHF progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: A joint analysis of the cardiomyocytes from the 2D differentiations and the Drakhlis et al. cardiac organoid was conducted to determine whether the TBX5-ISL1+HAND1+ cardiomyocyte population was indeed OFT CMs.
source: To determine whether this TBX5-ISL1+HAND1+ cardiomyocyte population was indeed OFT CMs, we conducted a joint analysis of the cardiomyocytes from our 2D differentiations and the Drakhlis et al., cardiac organoid.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis methods described.

claim: Using unsupervised clustering, a cardiomyocyte population emerged from the Drakhlis et al. study that displayed the absence of TBX5.
source: Using unsupervised clustering, we observed a cardiomyocyte population emerge from this study that displayed the absence of TBX5.
evidence: This claim is supported by the joint clustering analysis.

claim: The rest of the organoid cardiomyocytes co-clustered with the cells from the 2D differentiations indicating shared gene expression profiles.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the rest of the organoid cardiomyocytes co-clustered with the cells from our 2D differentiations indicating shared gene expression profiles (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the joint clustering analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis of the putative OFT CM cluster and the rest cardiomyocytes found a statistically significant enrichment of markers associated with OFT development including HAND1, BMP2, WNT5A, and PITX2.
source: We conducted differential gene expression analysis of the putative OFT CM cluster and the rest cardiomyocytes and found a statistically significant enrichment of markers associated with OFT development including HAND1, BMP2, WNT5A, and PITX2 (Délot et al., 2003; Li et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2013; Schleiffarth et al., 2007), while the rest of the cardiomyocytes exhibited high expression of markers associated with early LV development such as TBX5 and NPPA (Figure 6G, Figure 6—source data 1; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6G and citations to prior work on OFT markers.

claim: The rest of the cardiomyocytes exhibited high expression of markers associated with early LV development such as TBX5 and NPPA.
source: We conducted differential gene expression analysis of the putative OFT CM cluster and the rest cardiomyocytes and found a statistically significant enrichment of markers associated with OFT development including HAND1, BMP2, WNT5A, and PITX2 (Délot et al., 2003; Li et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2013; Schleiffarth et al., 2007), while the rest of the cardiomyocytes exhibited high expression of markers associated with early LV development such as TBX5 and NPPA (Figure 6G, Figure 6—source data 1; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6G and a citation to prior work.

claim: The data provide strong evidence for the emergence of a SHF-derived cell type within a 3D organoid differentiation protocol.
source: Overall, these data thus provide strong evidence for the emergence of a SHF-derived cell type within a 3D organoid differentiation protocol and reinforce the left ventricular identity that we identified using a standard 2D small molecule differentiation protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cumulative comparative analysis results.

claim: The data reinforce the left ventricular identity identified using a standard 2D small molecule differentiation protocol.
source: Overall, these data thus provide strong evidence for the emergence of a SHF-derived cell type within a 3D organoid differentiation protocol and reinforce the left ventricular identity that we identified using a standard 2D small molecule differentiation protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cumulative analysis results from the 2D differentiation experiments.
